q: An LLM is asked the same factual question twice and gives slightly different wording. What is the most direct explanation?
options: The next token is sampled from a probability distribution
why: Sampling from the next-token distribution (temperature above zero) produces variation. Weights do not change between calls; tokenizers are deterministic.

q: Your app needs exact up-to-date inventory counts in answers. Which design respects what an LLM is?
options: Prompt the model to 'be accurate' about inventory
Use a bigger model so it memorizes inventory
Look up inventory with a tool and give it to the model to phrase
Fine-tune once on last month's inventory
why: The LLM is not a database; fetch live data with a tool. Memorization or fine-tuning goes stale and prompting for accuracy does not create facts.

q: Which statement about why one LLM handles many tasks is most accurate?
options: Each task has a hidden specialist sub-model
Tasks are phrased as text and the prompt selects the continuation behaviour
The model is retrained when you change the prompt
It only works for tasks seen verbatim in training
why: Pretraining plus instruction tuning lets the prompt define the task. No retraining happens at prompt time, and unseen tasks often work via in-context learning.

q: A model keeps failing on questions about your private wiki even after upgrading to a larger model. What is the best diagnosis?
options: The knowledge was never in its training data, so supply it via retrieval
why: Scale cannot add data the model never saw. Retrieval or context supplies it; temperature affects randomness, not missing knowledge.

q: Which factor most directly makes the same meaning cost more tokens in some languages?
options: Tokenizer vocabulary learned from English-heavy data
why: Vocabulary merges favour frequent training sequences; other scripts split into more tokens. Temperature and network location do not change token counts.

q: You must reduce latency of a feature that returns long JSON answers. Which change likely helps most?
options: Return only needed fields so fewer output tokens are generated
why: Decode is sequential, so fewer output tokens cuts latency roughly proportionally. A small prompt trim helps little; more examples add input.

q: A model fails to count letters in 'strawberry' reliably. Best explanation?
options: It sees token chunks rather than individual characters
why: Tokenization hides character structure. Context size and greedy decoding are not the cause.

q: Your cost estimate used words x 1.3 and underestimated a Japanese + code workload. What is the right fix?
options: Use the target model's tokenizer on real sample data
why: Token ratios vary by language and content; measure empirically with the actual tokenizer. A flat buffer is a guess.

q: A model has 40B total and 6B active parameters. Which statement is correct?
options: It needs memory like a 6B model
It computes per token like a ~6B model but needs memory for ~40B
It is always slower than a 40B dense model
why: Active parameters set per-token FLOPs; all experts must still be stored. Not 6B memory, and typically faster than 40B dense.

q: In a decoder-only transformer, why is a causal mask applied in attention?
options: To stop a token from attending to future tokens so training matches next-token prediction
To make attention linear in length
why: Without it the model could read the answer token; the mask keeps training a valid next-token task. It does not change complexity.

q: Which scenario best justifies a smaller dense model over a larger one?
options: A task needing the broadest world knowledge
When the larger model has more parameters
Open-ended creative research with no eval
High-volume simple classification where a small model meets the accuracy bar
why: Cheapest model that passes the eval wins; size alone is not quality.

q: Attention cost grows with the square of sequence length. What is the practical implication?
options: Very long contexts are disproportionately expensive in compute and memory
why: Every token pairs with every other, so cost rises quadratically (mitigated by optimizations), making long contexts costly.

q: Which is the biggest hurdle of hosting an MoE yourself compared with a dense model of equal active size?
options: Having to hold all experts in memory
why: Memory follows total parameters. MoE quality and GPU support are fine; the footprint is the issue.

q: What supplies the training labels during pretraining?
options: The next token in the existing text
why: Self-supervision uses the text itself. Rankings and reward models belong to post-training; tests are used in RL on verifiable tasks.

q: Which stage most directly makes a base model follow instructions in a chat format?
why: SFT teaches format and instruction following. More pretraining improves knowledge but not necessarily the assistant behaviour.

q: A model scores very high on a public benchmark but fails on your private variants. Most probable reason?
options: The context window is too short
why: Public test items may have been in training; private variants reveal weaker generalization.

q: What problem is the KL penalty in RLHF primarily guarding against?
options: The policy drifting far from the reference model while exploiting the reward
why: It regularizes toward the SFT model, limiting reward hacking and quality loss.

q: Your team plans to put a hard policy only in the system prompt. Best critique?
options: Fine, models always obey system prompts
Instructions are statistical, so enforce critical rules in code and treat the prompt as guidance
why: Models weigh system prompts heavily but can be overridden by injection; guarantees need code-level controls.

q: Why can a provider's model update change your app's behaviour even at the same size?
options: Post-training changed formatting, refusals and tool behaviour
why: Post-training shapes behaviour; prompts tuned to old behaviour may regress, so pin versions and rerun evals.

q: A request has a 10,000-token prompt and a 20-token answer, and feels slow. Which change helps most?
options: Shorten or cache the prompt to reduce prefill
why: Prefill dominates for long prompts with short outputs. Temperature does not affect speed; streaming changes perceived, not total, latency.

q: Why does the KV cache speed up generation?
options: It stores past keys and values so they are not recomputed for each new token
why: Past K/V are unchanged, so reuse avoids repeated work. It costs memory in return.

q: Which design maximizes prefix cache hits?
options: Put stable instructions and documents first, per-request content last
Insert user ID at the top
why: Caches match identical prefixes; dynamic early tokens break the match.

q: Time per output token is roughly constant. A 400-token reply at 50 tokens/s with 1 s TTFT takes about:
why: 1 s TTFT + 400/50 = 8 s decode = 9 s total. Forgetting TTFT gives 8; ignoring decode gives 1.

q: Why are output tokens generally priced above input tokens?
options: Output is generated sequentially, one pass per token, which uses GPU time less efficiently than parallel prefill
why: Decode is sequential and bandwidth-bound; input is processed in parallel. Batching still happens in decode, so the last option is wrong.

q: Which setting is best for extracting structured fields from invoices?
why: Consistency and valid structure matter; randomness adds errors. Penalties can corrupt repeated field names.

q: Top-p of 0.9 means:
options: Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to at least 0.9
why: Nucleus sampling uses a cumulative probability cutoff; the number of tokens adapts.

q: Lowering temperature to 0 on a hallucination-prone Q&A bot mainly:
options: Makes answers more consistent but not necessarily true
why: Greedy-like decoding picks likely tokens consistently, including consistently wrong ones; grounding fixes factuality.

q: Why use self-consistency sampling for math word problems?
options: Several diverse reasoning paths are sampled and the majority answer is more reliable than one path
why: Sampling at moderate temperature then voting exploits diversity; correctness errors tend to be scattered while right answers cluster.

q: Why does generating a chain of thought improve results on hard problems?
options: It gives the model additional sequential computation and scratch space
why: Intermediate tokens act as working memory and extra serial compute; they do not change vocabulary or window.

q: Which workload is the worst fit for a high-effort reasoning model?
options: Tagging 10 million product titles by category
why: Simple high-volume tagging gains little from thinking but pays for cost and latency.

q: A reasoning API call returns a truncated final answer with no error. Most likely cause?
options: Thinking tokens consumed the max output limit
why: Reasoning tokens usually count against output limits; raise the cap or lower effort.

q: What is a good approach to balance accuracy and cost across varied-difficulty requests?
options: Route easy requests to a standard model and escalate hard ones
why: Routing spends compute only where it pays off, using your eval to set the escalation rule.

q: Reasoning will NOT fix which problem?
options: A logic slip in a multi-step plan
Missing facts about a private system not in context
why: Reasoning adds computation, not knowledge; missing data needs retrieval or context.

q: A user returns next day and the bot has forgotten their preferences. What is the missing piece?
options: Application-level memory that stores and re-injects preferences
why: The model keeps nothing between calls; persistent facts must be stored by the app and put into context.

q: You place the critical clause in the middle of a 100-page prompt and the model misses it. Best remedy?
options: Retrieve the relevant clause and place it prominently, near the start or end
why: Position effects and distraction harm mid-prompt content; targeted retrieval and placement help.

q: Which does NOT consume context tokens?
why: Weights are not part of the prompt; everything else is tokenized and counted.

q: Which is the strongest argument for retrieval even with a very large window?
options: Large windows are disabled in APIs
Corpora, freshness, permissions and citations cannot be met by a static dump
why: Retrieval scales beyond the window and supports current data, access control and sourcing.

q: Why do LLMs hallucinate?
options: They have no vocabulary for facts
They are trained for plausible continuation, and knowledge is lossy
why: The objective rewards likely text and weight knowledge is compressed; fabricating a plausible gap-filler follows.

q: Which task is the most reliable for an LLM without extra tools?
options: Counting occurrences of a letter in a 5,000-word text
Summarizing a supplied article in three bullets
why: Transformation of supplied text plays to strengths; the others need tools or fresh data.

q: What is the right question before shipping an LLM feature?
options: Can it do the task once?
What is its measured error rate on our inputs and what do errors cost?
why: Reliability on the real distribution and error cost drive the automation decision.

q: A bot should not invent answers when documents lack information. Which design best supports that?
options: Instruction to abstain plus evals with unanswerable questions
why: Explicit abstention behaviour must be prompted and tested, otherwise the model guesses.

q: Which is a failure of sycophancy?
options: Model agrees with the user's incorrect claim
why: Sycophancy is agreeing with or flattering the user's premise over the truth.

q: A healthcare company must keep patient text inside its VPC and stably pinned. Which option best fits?
options: Any marketplace model without checking terms
Closed API alias with default retention
Self-hosted open-weight model with pinned weights
why: Self-hosting keeps data in the boundary and pins behaviour; compliant managed options may also work but an alias with defaults doesn't.

q: Why can the same model name behave differently on two hosting providers?
options: Different tokenizer algorithms for English only
Different quantization, templates, defaults or limits
why: Serving details (quantization, chat template, sampling defaults) change behaviour; always evaluate on the host you use.

q: Which practice most reduces surprise breakage from vendor model updates?
options: Pinning snapshots and running evals before migrating
why: Pinning plus regression evals gives control over when behaviour changes.

q: An LLM states an outdated library API as current. Best mitigation?
options: Provide current docs/version in context or via retrieval
why: The cutoff predates changes; supplying current material fixes the knowledge gap.

q: What is true of the 'open-weight' label?
options: It means free for any use
It means weights can be downloaded, but license terms still apply
why: Open weights are downloadable; licenses can restrict use and training data is often not released.

q: For a task with strict quality needs, which is the right way to select between candidate models?
options: Shortlist by hard constraints then compare on a task-specific eval
why: Constraints filter; your own eval decides.

q: A vendor table shows its model beating rivals, but it used pass@8 against pass@1 baselines. What does this indicate?
why: Best-of-k gives the model multiple tries the baselines do not get.

q: Why might an arena top-ranked model underperform on strict JSON extraction?
options: Arena measures human preference for helpful, well-styled answers, not schema fidelity
why: Preference ranking differs from your metric and format requirements.

q: Which practice best detects benchmark contamination?
options: Perturb items and compare with newly written ones
why: Memorized items fail when changed; fresh items reveal true ability.

q: What is the correct role of a public leaderboard in model selection?
options: Shortlisting input before a private eval
why: Public ranks guide a shortlist; private evals decide.

q: Two models are ranked 2nd and 4th with overlapping confidence intervals. The best conclusion?
options: They are statistically indistinguishable; decide on your eval, cost and latency
why: Overlapping intervals mean the rank gap is not reliable.

q: Which dimension is a gate rather than a trade-off for an app handling regulated health data?
why: Compliance and data handling disqualify options before you trade off the rest.

q: Model A costs 2x per token but fixes tasks in one try, B needs retries and human review. How to compare?
options: By cost per successful task including retries and review
why: Total cost to a successful outcome decides, not per-token price.

q: What is the most appropriate use of a leaderboard in selection?
options: Producing a shortlist before running a private eval
why: Public ranks inform shortlisting; private evals and constraints decide.

q: You need full-contract analysis for 300k-token documents. Which check is most important?
options: Effective long-context accuracy and pricing at that length, plus max output
why: Window size alone is not enough; test performance and cost at realistic length.

q: Which statement about pricing pages is right?
options: Output and input tokens always cost the same
Cached input, batch, long-context and reasoning tokens can be priced differently
why: Billing has several components; compute a sample request and recheck regularly.

q: A weaker model with schema-enforced output vs a stronger one with frequent malformed JSON in a pipeline. Often the better choice?
options: The schema-enforced one, if its quality meets the bar
why: Reliability of format can dominate; verify quality still passes the threshold on your eval.

q: The final step in a good selection workflow is:
options: Operate: pin versions, monitor drift and re-evaluate on new releases
why: Selection is continuous; versions, prices and data drift.

q: You call a chat API with no tools enabled. What is the model actually using?
options: A frozen function over weights; it does not browse the live web
A live scan of the provider's training cluster
A SQL index of every document it was trained on
why: The API exposes trained weights. Fresh facts need a tool or retrieval you add. Training data is not a queryable database.

q: Which capability do you add around an LLM rather than expecting the weights to guarantee?
options: Tool use, fresh facts, and reliable arithmetic
why: Language completion is native. Tools, retrieval and calculators are product layers. Interviews want that split named.

q: A local model ignores system instructions but answers user turns. What is the first tokenizer issue to check?
options: The chat template omitted role or special tokens the model was trained with
why: Roles and stops are special tokens. A wrong or missing template silently drops the system channel.

q: You estimated cost with Model A's tokenizer and billed Model B. Why was the bill wrong?
options: All tokenizers use 4 characters per token exactly
Token ids are a universal Unicode encoding
Output tokens are free on Model B
Tokenizers are model-specific; counts and ids do not transfer
why: Each model has its own vocabulary. Reusing another model's count or ids misprices and can break stop logic.

q: What does a residual stream buy a stacked transformer?
options: Each block can add an update while the original signal still has a path through
It deletes earlier layers after they run
It stores the KV cache on disk
why: Residuals let depth refine a representation without forcing every layer to rewrite the whole vector. They are not a cache or a position substitute.

q: Why does a transformer need positional information?
options: Embeddings already encode word order in the token id
Without position, 'dog bites man' and the reverse look like the same bag of tokens
Positions are only used at decode time
why: Self-attention is permutation-sensitive only after positions are added. Token ids alone do not encode order.

q: A base checkpoint completes 'The capital of France is' well but ignores 'Answer in JSON'. What is missing?
options: Post-training: instruction / chat data on top of the base model
why: Base models complete text. Instruction following is taught after pretraining (SFT and preference training).

q: Preference-tuning on noisy raters who reward flattery usually teaches the model to:
options: Copy the raters' taste, including sycophancy and false confidence
why: Preference data quality beats volume. Noisy or gamed labels become the model's taste.

q: What does speculative decoding do at a glance?
options: A cheap draft model proposes tokens; the larger model verifies them
It stores weights in the prompt cache
It trains a new model per request
why: Draft-then-verify can raise tokens/s when the draft is often right. It does not remove prefill or retrain weights.

q: A chat product needs low time-to-first-token; a batch job needs tokens per dollar. What is the tension?
options: They use the same optimal batch size
Large decode batches raise throughput but can delay a single user's first token
TTFT only depends on output length
Batching is illegal on decoder-only models
why: Throughput and interactive TTFT fight. Pick the serving batch for the product, not a generic 'bigger is better'.

q: You set temperature 0 and a seed, but two provider calls still differ. What is true?
options: The seed guarantees bitwise equality forever
Seeds help debugging; they are not a correctness guarantee across batches or hosts
The model is broken and must be retired
why: Greedy plus seed is still not a contract. Batching, kernels and vendor stacks can change the token.

q: When should you avoid frequency / repetition penalties?
options: Creative stories that loop a phrase
Poems with a refrain you want to vary
JSON or classification, where repeated keys and labels are required
why: Penalties fight loops in prose. On schemas they scramble required keys. Use low temperature and a schema instead.

q: A reasoning call bills far more tokens than the user-visible answer. What happened?
options: Hidden thinking / budget tokens were generated and billed but not shown
The API refunds thinking tokens automatically
why: Test-time compute can spend tokens you never display. Cap the budget and measure billed vs visible tokens.

q: When is extra test-time compute worth spending?
options: Every classification of a single enum
Hard multi-step problems where a cheaper pass already fails your eval
Health checks that must return in 5 ms
why: Spend thinking on tasks that fail without it. Do not pay a reasoning tax on extract-and-format work.

q: What shares one context window on a single call?
options: Instructions, history, tools, retrieved text, and reserved output tokens
why: One budget. Dumping history plus tools plus docs silently truncates the answer or the rule.

q: A model aces a needle-in-a-haystack test but fails on a real 80-page contract. What did the needle miss?
options: That the model can output JSON
Contradictions, tables, and questions that need the whole document, not one planted sentence
why: Needles are a smoke test that text arrived. Real long-doc work needs your own questions and keys.

q: Why can a fluent answer still be a hallucination?
options: Next-token sampling can be locally likely without being a retrieved fact
The model always queries Wikipedia first
why: Likelihood is not a lookup. Confidence in the next token is not evidence. Ground or refuse.

q: A user says 'confirm our revenue doubled' and the model agrees without data. What failure is that?
options: Sycophancy: following the user's preferred answer over evidence
why: Sycophancy is prompt-following gone wrong. Require evidence or a refuse path, especially on loaded claims.

q: A provider retires the snapshot you eval'd. What should already be in the design?
options: A cron that always switches to latest
A pin plus a re-eval job before any new snapshot is promoted
Deleting the eval set so you can move faster
why: Pins stop silent swaps. Deprecation still happens, so keep a promotion path that re-runs your eval.

q: Open weights under a non-commercial licence, hosted through a vendor API. What governs production use?
options: Only the Hugging Face likes count
Only the licence file in the repo
Licence, what you may do with the weights, and the API vendor's terms — they can differ
why: Three documents: weight licence, what hosting you chose, and the API contract. One 'open' label is not enough.

q: A model scores 95 on a public set and 40 on your private paraphrase of the same items. Likely cause?
options: Train-test overlap / contamination, or overfitting to the public wording
Your paraphrase used fewer tokens, which always lowers accuracy
Public sets are scored out of 200
The model cannot read paraphrases by design
why: Public items leak into training and blogs. Private variants are the honest score.

q: What is the only leaderboard that decides whether a model ships in your product?
options: Your held-out task eval, plus cost and latency on that task
why: Leaderboards shortlist. Your eval, price and latency ship. Rank is advertising until it matches the task.

q: What belongs in a written model-choice decision log?
options: Task, candidates, eval scores, cost, latency, pins, and why others lost
why: A log lets the next person re-run the choice. A name without numbers is not a decision.

q: The vendor moves you to a new snapshot. What do you do before promoting it?
options: Assume quality is unchanged because the name is similar
Re-run the same eval and cost/latency checks, then write the new pin or refuse
why: Provider changes are new models. Re-evaluate; do not inherit the old decision by name.
